characters: Maame Pokua: a wise older Ghanaian woman wearing an ochre-gold headscarf and earth-toned wrapper cloth, carrying a small clay smoke pot and a round woven basket.
Her neighbour: an impatient man in a bright green shirt and brown trousers.
Bees: golden-brown honeybees buzzing around natural hives high in tall forest-edge trees and farm blossoms.

narrationPlan.voice: A warm storyteller; a wise, calm voice for Maame Pokua; a loud, boasting voice for the neighbour
narrationPlan.pace: Warm storytelling pace, firmer on the closing lesson (about 85 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A gentle buzzing hum and a warm kalimba (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Harvesting wild honey and keeping traditional hives are real livelihoods in forest and savanna communities across Ghana. This is a newly written moral tale in the folktale style, not an ancient traditional story.
Honeybees pollinate many fruit trees and farm crops. (Cocoa flowers are pollinated mainly by tiny midges, so this story focuses accurately on fruit trees.)
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm that the honey-gathering details (smoke pot, dry season) fit local practice.
Ensure readers know this is a newly written moral tale in folktale style, as stated in the summary and notes.

teacherGuide.overview: A newly written moral tale about sustainable harvesting and leaving enough for nature to thrive, linking fair sharing with pollination in science.
learningGoals: State the moral of the story in your own words.
Explain why Maame Pokua leaves half of the honey.
Describe how bees help fruit trees grow fruit.
beforeReading: Ask: where does honey come from, and what else do bees do for farms?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and ask children whose advice seems wiser and why.
afterReading: Draw the two tree hives side by side: the cared-for hive and the empty hive.
Tell a short story about sharing water, fish, or firewood fairly.
discussion: What is the difference between taking what you need and taking everything?
reflection: How can we avoid wasting food or water at home and at school?

support: Fold a paper circle in half to show “half for me, half for the bees”.
stretch: Explain how Maame Pokua’s rule also applies to fishing in a river or cutting firewood.

culturalNotes: Harvesting wild honey and keeping traditional hives are real livelihoods in forest and savanna communities across Ghana. This is a newly written moral tale in the folktale style, not an ancient traditional story.
Honeybees pollinate many fruit trees and farm crops. (Cocoa flowers are pollinated mainly by tiny midges, so this story focuses accurately on fruit trees.)
localiseThis: Use local names for honeybees and familiar local fruit trees.
Remind learners that honeybees sting and only trained adults with protective methods harvest honey.
